subsection: 1. The Second Reich, Bismarck's foreign policy and the changing balance of power, 1871–1890

notes.b: The German Empire was proclaimed in 1871 after the Prussian-led wars of unification. It combined a powerful monarchy with an elected parliament and a federal council of states.
points: The German Empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871 in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, during the Franco-Prussian War.
The Kaiser was hereditary and was also King of Prussia; the title passed to Wilhelm I in 1871.
The Chancellor was appointed by the Kaiser and was responsible to him, not to the Reichstag.
The Reichstag was elected by universal male suffrage for men aged 25 and over, but it could not appoint or dismiss ministers.
The Bundesrat (federal council) represented the states; Prussia held 17 of its 58 votes, giving it a controlling position.
The Franco-Prussian peace of Frankfurt (May 1871) required France to pay an indemnity of 5 billion francs and cede Alsace and most of Lorraine to Germany.

notes.b: Bismarck's central foreign policy aim was to keep the new Reich secure by preventing a coalition of powers against it. He also needed to keep France isolated, because France wanted to recover Alsace-Lorraine.
points: French nationalists sought revanche, meaning revenge for 1871 and the recovery of Alsace-Lorraine, and this made France the main potential enemy.
Bismarck described Germany as a satiated power, meaning one that wanted no further territory in Europe.
His preferred method was a web of treaties that kept Austria-Hungary, Russia, Italy and Britain on good terms with Germany.
Bismarck also kept direct control of foreign policy, so decisions were taken by the Chancellor rather than by the Reichstag or the Foreign Office alone.

notes.h: Crisis of 1875 and the Three Emperors' League
points: In spring 1875 German newspapers, under Bismarck's influence, suggested that France was rearming too fast and might be attacked; this became known as the War-in-Sight crisis.
Russia and Britain both intervened diplomatically to restrain Germany, which showed that other powers would resist German dominance.
The Three Emperors' League of October 1873 linked Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia in a conservative understanding against revolution.
The League lapsed after the Russo-Turkish War and the Congress of Berlin, when Russia and Austria-Hungary clashed over the Balkans.
It was renewed in 1881, but Russia's distrust of Austria-Hungary made it weaker than before.

notes.h: The Congress of Berlin and the Dual Alliance
notes.b: The Balkan settlement of 1878 and the alliance of 1879 marked the start of the German commitment to Austria-Hungary.
points: The Congress of Berlin (June to July 1878) revised the Treaty of San Stefano, which had greatly enlarged Russian influence in the Balkans.
At Berlin, Bismarck presented himself as an impartial mediator rather than as a participant with interests of his own.
Austria-Hungary was given the right to occupy Bosnia-Herzegovina, which Russia had hoped to share in and which Austria would annex in 1908.
The Dual Alliance (7 October 1879) was a secret defensive agreement between Germany and Austria-Hungary, under which each would support the other if attacked by Russia.
If one partner were attacked by a different power, the other was only pledged to stay neutral.
Russia's resentment at the Congress and at the Dual Alliance pushed it towards closer ties with France in the following decade.

notes.h: The Triple Alliance and the Reinsurance Treaty
points: Italy joined the Dual Alliance in May 1882, creating the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy.
Italy's motive was rivalry with France over North Africa, especially after France occupied Tunisia in 1881.
The Triple Alliance was defensive, and Italy's commitment was weaker than Austria-Hungary's, because Italy hoped to stay out of a war with Britain.
The Reinsurance Treaty of June 1887 bound Germany and Russia to neutrality if either was attacked, unless Germany attacked France or Russia attacked Austria-Hungary.
The treaty was secret, and Bismarck kept it from Austria-Hungary, which showed the strain within his system.
The treaty's purpose was to keep Russia from allying with France, which would have left Germany facing a two-front war.

notes.h: Colonial acquisitions and relations with Britain, 1884–1885
points: Bismarck's colonial policy began in 1884 with the acquisition of South West Africa (now Namibia), Togoland and the Cameroons.
German East Africa was claimed in 1885, extending German territory on the east coast of Africa.
Bismarck used colonial claims partly as a bargaining tool with France and Britain, rather than as a long-term programme of empire.
The colonial moves caused friction with Britain over African claims, but Bismarck wanted to keep Britain friendly and avoided a serious rupture.
The Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 that regulated European claims in Africa is covered in the notes on the New Imperialism and colonial rivalries.

notes.b: Bismarck shaped German unification in the 1860s and then governed the Reich as its first Chancellor until 1890. The notes on unification cover his earlier career; this block covers his Chancellorship.
points: Bismarck was born on 1 April 1815 at Schönhausen in Prussia and came from a Junker landowning family.

He became Minister-President of Prussia in September 1862, when he told the Prussian parliament that the great questions of the day would be decided by blood and iron rather than by speeches and majority votes.
Bismarck was Chancellor of the German Empire from 1871 to March 1890, and he dominated German politics and foreign policy throughout this period.
He was Chancellor under two emperors: Wilhelm I, who died in March 1888, and Frederick III, who ruled for only 99 days in 1888 before dying of cancer.
Bismarck was dismissed by Wilhelm II on 18 March 1890 after disputes over domestic policy and the Kaiser's wish to rule personally.
Contemporaries saw him as the Iron Chancellor who had made Germany a great power; German nationalists admired him, while Liberals, Catholics and socialists opposed his domestic measures.
He died on 30 July 1898 at Friedrichsruh, having written memoirs that defended his record.

Historians disagree on his legacy: some praise his restraint and skill in keeping the peace after 1871, while others argue that his alliance network and domestic repression built the tensions that later exploded.

notes.b: Bismarck's system is judged both by what it achieved and by what it left behind.
points: Achievement: Germany avoided a war with any major power for two decades after 1871, which contemporaries and many later historians credit to Bismarck's diplomacy.
Limit: the system depended on Bismarck personally, and it collapsed or became unworkable once he left office in 1890.
Achievement: the Dual Alliance and the Triple Alliance tied Germany to Austria-Hungary and Italy, providing security against Russia and France.
Limit: the same alliances committed Germany to supporting Austria-Hungary in the Balkans, where Russian and Austrian interests clashed.
Achievement: the Berlin Congress of 1878 was a successful peace conference that prevented an immediate Russo-Austrian war over the Balkans.
Limit: the Reinsurance Treaty gave Russia an assurance that contradicted the Dual Alliance, which later made the alliance system harder to manage.

keyTerms.definition: A situation in which no single state is strong enough to dominate Europe, and rival states form alliances to prevent any one of them from doing so.
The German Empire founded in 1871, which combined the Kaiser and Chancellor with a federal council and an elected Reichstag.
The German parliament, elected by universal male suffrage, which could pass laws but could not appoint or dismiss the Chancellor.
The federal council of the German Empire, representing the individual states, in which Prussia held the largest number of votes.
The French desire for revenge against Germany and the recovery of Alsace-Lorraine after the Franco-Prussian War.
The 1873 understanding between Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia to cooperate in preserving conservative government and peace in Europe.
The secret 1879 defensive alliance between Germany and Austria-Hungary, directed against an attack by Russia.
The 1882 defensive alliance linking Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy.
The secret 1887 agreement between Germany and Russia, promising neutrality if either was attacked, which Bismarck kept hidden from Austria-Hungary.

factCards.term: Where and when was the German Empire proclaimed?
factCards.definition: At Versailles on 18 January 1871, during the Franco-Prussian War.

factCards.term: What did the Frankfurt peace of May 1871 impose on France?
factCards.definition: An indemnity of 5 billion francs, and the cession of Alsace and most of Lorraine to Germany.
The spring 1875 scare, stirred by German press comment, that France was preparing for war; Russia and Britain intervened to restrain Germany.

factCards.term: Which powers were the Three Emperors' League members?
factCards.definition: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia, linked by the 1873 agreement.

factCards.term: Which two states formed the Dual Alliance of 1879?
factCards.definition: Germany and Austria-Hungary, which agreed to support each other if Russia attacked either of them.

factCards.term: Which state joined the Dual Alliance in 1882 and why?
factCards.definition: Italy, which hoped to counter French influence in North Africa, especially after France occupied Tunisia in 1881.

factCards.term: What did the Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 promise?
factCards.definition: Neutrality between Germany and Russia if either was attacked, with exceptions for attacks on France or Austria-Hungary.

factCards.term: Which German colonies were claimed in 1884?
factCards.definition: South West Africa (now Namibia), Togoland and the Cameroons, with German East Africa following in 1885.

factCards.term: When and where was the Congress of Berlin held?
factCards.definition: In June and July 1878 in Berlin, where Bismarck acted as an impartial mediator over the Balkans.

factCards.term: How did Bismarck leave office, and when?
factCards.definition: He was dismissed by Wilhelm II on 18 March 1890, after disputes over domestic policy and the Kaiser's wish to rule personally.

factCards.term: What did Bismarck mean by blood and iron?
factCards.definition: His 1862 claim, made to the Prussian parliament, that the great questions would be settled by force rather than by parliamentary votes.
Of representatives of the German states, with Prussia holding 17 of its 58 votes.
